---
title: "What changes when the data is not on your laptop"
subtitle: "The one shift behind almost every surprise on this site"
---

Read this once and the rest of the site gets shorter. Nearly every trap documented here is the same assumption failing, and it is an assumption worth naming because on your laptop it was true.

## What has changed

On your own machine, "where does this run" is not a question anyone asks, because there is nothing to ask about. One machine, one R session, one filesystem. A package you installed is installed. An object in your environment is there. A file path points at a file.

None of that needed thinking about, and none of it was wrong. Four of those assumptions now break, and the order matters, because each one depends on the one before. A fifth section follows them, on running R where the data is, which is a mechanism rather than an assumption.

## There is more than one machine

The first and the largest. Your R session is on one machine, the data is on another, and there may be several more behind it.

The vocabulary is worth having, once, because you will meet it in error messages and vendor documentation. The machine that coordinates is the **driver**. Machines that do work in parallel are **workers** or **executors**, used more or less interchangeably.

Your cluster may have exactly one machine, in which case the driver is also the only place work can happen. That is a common and perfectly ordinary arrangement rather than a broken one, and it changes what is worth attempting: [Work out what the cluster you have can do](../howdoi/compute.qmd) tells you which you have, and it is the first thing to find out.

Everything below is a consequence of this section.

## Your session is a client, not a place the work happens

This is the distinction that catches people. Connecting to Databricks does not move your R session onto Databricks. Your session stays exactly where it is and sends instructions.

So there are two machines with two different jobs, and the interesting question about any line of your code is which one it ran on. A `dplyr` pipeline against a remote table builds a query and sends it; the filtering happens over there. `collect()` is the moment the answer comes back, and it is the only moment data crosses.

That is why the pipeline in [Work with a table that will not fit in your session](../howdoi/big-table.qmd) has a line through the middle of it, and why "the data is too big to fit" and "the data is too big to move" are different problems with different answers.

## Anything the far side needs has to get there, and that costs something

If the work happens on another machine, then the function you wrote, the objects it refers to, and any file it reads all have to travel. Converting them to bytes, shipping them, and rebuilding them on the far side is called **serialisation**, and it is the one platform word worth knowing properly, because it is the hidden term in most performance surprises.

The consequence is counterintuitive, and the site relies on it repeatedly: distributing work is not free, so distributing something small can be slower than not distributing it at all. That is not a misconfiguration. It is the cost being larger than the saving.

Getting a specific object to the far side is a practical problem with a practical answer, which is [Sending things to where your code runs](../ref/sending-things.qmd).

## Each context has its own library

The last one, and the one that produces the most confusing symptoms.

"Installed" is not a property of the cluster. It is a property of a particular R context, and there are several: your session, the cluster's driver, and each worker. A package that loads in your session says nothing about whether it loads in a worker. An install may not survive to the next session at all.

This is why an upgrade can appear not to have taken. It did take, and then the library went away, so running it again produces the same result. [Packages](../ref/packages.qmd) exists as a separate page for this reason, and has the check to run in each context.

## Running R where the data is

`spark_apply()` is how you send an R function to run on the cluster rather than in your session. It belongs here rather than inside any one task, because it turns up in several: it is a mechanism, like `collect()`, not a step in a particular recipe.

You give it a table and a function, and the function runs over on the cluster against pieces of that table. What comes back is a table.

The parts of this differ in how well established they are, so:

- **Across worker machines, it distributes.** Observed on a two-worker cluster by counting distinct machine names, with real geospatial work running on both. That answers whether it distributes and nothing else. Nothing here speaks to shuffle cost, or to behaviour at twenty nodes.
- **On a single-node cluster it was slower than forked parallel workers**, by roughly a factor of two, because it pays the serialisation cost for distribution it cannot deliver. That is the previous section made concrete.
- **Inside a `dplyr` pipeline** is something people do, and it has not been verified here. Treat it as untested rather than as established.
- **Naming the output columns depends on where you are.** A Spark type string from a client connection, a plain character vector on the cluster's own R session. Neither form is rejected by the other path and the error never names the argument, so it surfaces as a missing column and looks like a fault in your function. Omitting `columns` works on both.
- **The grouped path does not run** on a current runtime: `spark_apply(group_by = ...)` fails on `rpy2` 3.6.x. Use the partition-based form and do the grouping inside your function.

Where it is worth reaching for, and where it is not, belongs on the task pages that use it. [Run a Monte Carlo simulation](../howdoi/monte-carlo.qmd) is the fullest treatment.

## What this buys you

The four assumptions map onto the symptoms you will actually meet, which makes this page a diagnostic aid rather than theory.

If a package will not load, that is the fourth: ask which context you are in. If something is slower than you expected, usually the third: work is being shipped somewhere, or shipped somewhere with nowhere to go. If a result is empty, truncated or the wrong shape, often the second: something ran on a side you did not intend. And if none of it makes sense yet, the first: find out how many machines you have.
